title: AMBER: Training Long-Horizon Web Agents through Append-Only Memory
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 5 Oct 2026]
Title:AMBER: Training Long-Horizon Web Agents through Append-Only Memory
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Modern language-model agents increasingly interact with external environments over long-horizon, multi-step trajectories, where the accumulated interaction history can quickly exceed practical context budgets. To ensure reliability, agents must maintain factual information over long horizons, remember execution errors and corrective feedback, and track progress across actions. Several approaches have been proposed to achieve this without the need for maintaining the entire execution history in context, such as using the reasoning and action history, learning to maintain a fixed-size memory through an overwrite mechanism, and periodic summarization. Although overwrite memory can in principle retain anything an append-only memory can, it must learn to carry each fact through every subsequent rewrite, which is difficult to learn from sparse outcome rewards; for interactive applications like web agents, we find that trained overwrite memories delete key information required by the trajectory, as well as corrective feedback received from the environment. We introduce AMBER (Append-only Memory Bank for Evidence Retention) - a simple and scalable framework where an agent jointly learns to reason, act, and write free-form memory, while an append-only rule guarantees retention by construction. This allows AMBER to be trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning from outcome rewards without the need for extensive curated SFT data. On WebArena Lite, AMBER improves average success over overwrite-based memory by 4.09 percentage points, increases the fraction of tasks solved in five repeated runs by 4.8 percentage points, and matches an overwrite baseline trained on substantially more expensive curated supervision. AMBER achieves these improvements while maintaining a practical token budget, providing a strong balance between context efficiency, task performance, and reliable long-horizon execution.

report.summary: AMBER, an append-only memory framework, helps long-horizon web agents retain evidence and beats overwrite-based memory on WebArena Lite via reinforcement learning.
report.background: LLM-based web agents increasingly operate over long, multi-step trajectories — browsing, clicking, filling forms, recovering from errors. Each step adds observations to the context window, so histories quickly exceed practical token budgets, driving up cost and degrading reliability. Existing fixes include feeding full reasoning-and-action histories, periodic summarization, and learned fixed-size memory with an overwrite mechanism, in which the agent decides what to keep and what to discard at every rewrite. Overwrite memory is theoretically more expressive, but it must learn to carry each fact faithfully through every subsequent rewrite — a skill that is hard to acquire from sparse, outcome-only rewards. The authors observe that trained overwrite memories tend to drop facts the trajectory still needs, along with corrective feedback from the environment, motivating a retention-by-construction design.
key_points: AMBER stands for Append-Only Memory Bank for Evidence Retention: the agent jointly learns to reason, act, and write free-form memory notes, while an append-only rule prevents any stored entry from being deleted or overwritten.

Because retention is guaranteed by the architecture rather than learned, AMBER can be trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning from outcome rewards alone, avoiding expensive curated supervised fine-tuning data.
On WebArena Lite, AMBER improves average task success by 4.09 percentage points over overwrite-based memory and raises the fraction of tasks solved across five repeated runs by 4.8 percentage points.
It matches an overwrite baseline that was trained with substantially more expensive curated supervision, showing that the memory constraint is a cheaper substitute for heavy labeling.
AMBER keeps token usage within a practical budget, offering a balance between context efficiency, task performance, and reliable long-horizon execution.
report.impact: For the AI industry, AMBER argues that memory architecture — not just model scale — is a lever for agent reliability, and that a simple structural constraint can outperform a more expressive learned policy when rewards are sparse. For developers, it lowers the cost of building long-horizon agents: no elaborate memory-curation pipeline or distillation dataset is required, just outcome rewards and an append-only store, which is easy to bolt onto existing ReAct-style or browser-agent loops. It also reframes evaluation: repeated-run consistency, not single-run success, becomes a key metric. For regular users, the practical effect is agents that remember earlier instructions, errors, and corrections during multi-step tasks like booking, form-filling, or research, dropping fewer details mid-task and needing fewer restarts. Costs could also fall, since unbounded history no longer has to be re-fed to the model.
report.tools: To follow up, look at WebArena and its WebArena Lite split for benchmarking browser agents, and BrowserGym for standardized agent environments. For memory implementations, see Letta (formerly MemGPT), mem0, and LangGraph/LangChain memory stores, which can be adapted to append-only designs. For RL training of agents, consider verl, OpenRLHF, or TRL. The AMBER paper's reference list on arXiv, plus alphaXiv and Connected Papers, are useful for tracking related memory and agent-training work.
